items.q: How do you build a home-screen widget with Glance? What are its constraints compared to a Compose screen?
shortAnswer: Glance is a Compose-like DSL compiling down to `RemoteViews`: describe a `GlanceAppWidget` with `provideGlance`/`GlanceComposable`, backed by a `GlanceAppWidgetReceiver`.
There's no recomposition loop — you push state by calling `update(context, glanceId)`, and the composition runs synchronously to emit `RemoteViews`.
The constraints are real: input is clicks via `PendingIntent` only, the component set is small, and you must handle launcher sizing with `SizeMode`.
items.answer:
#### What Glance is
Glance is Jetpack's Compose-like API for home-screen widgets. It is not Compose running on your GPU — it is a DSL that describes a widget and is compiled to a **RemoteViews** hierarchy. A widget is a `GlanceAppWidget` subclass plus a `GlanceAppWidgetReceiver`, and its UI is declared in a `GlanceComposable` block inside `provideGlance`.

#### The rendering and update model
There is no recomposition in the Compose sense. State that should appear on the widget is pushed from your app — or from a WorkManager job, because app processes get killed — by calling `update(context, glanceId)`. The composition then runs synchronously to produce RemoteViews, so it must be fast and free of blocking work.

#### The constraints to know
Input is clicks only: `clickable` launches a `PendingIntent`, which must be `FLAG_IMMUTABLE`. The component set is deliberately small (Box, Column, Row, Text, Button, Image, and a few more). Sizing is explicit: `SizeMode.Exact`, `SizeMode.Responsive`, or `SizeMode.Single`, because a launcher grid can resize your widget. Glance's recent releases have expanded the surface, but the RemoteViews ceiling is permanent — no custom layouts, no arbitrary drawing.

#### When to use it
For glanceable views of existing state — a timer, a tracker, a trip summary. If you need rich interactive behavior, that is a signal to link back into the app rather than fight the widget surface.

code.caption: A Glance widget, its receiver, and how you push updates

followUps: Why does Glance render with RemoteViews instead of running real Compose?
How do you keep a widget updated when the app process is dead — say a long-running timer?
What happens when the launcher resizes your widget, and how do you handle it?
traps: Treating Glance as a full Compose runtime — custom layouts, arbitrary drawing, and recomposition do not exist there.
Forgetting that every interaction is a PendingIntent, and handing out a mutable one.

items.topic: Wear OS, TV, Auto and XR
items.q: You have a mature phone app. What changes when you add Wear OS, Android TV, Android Auto, and Android XR?
shortAnswer: The domain, data, and ViewModel layers survive untouched — what changes is the input model, the UI toolkit, and each surface's hard constraints.
Wear brings rotary input, complications, and ambient mode; TV is D-pad focus; Auto allows only distraction-safe templates; XR renders Compose UI as spatial panels.
The gating factor is adaptive design first: if the phone app doesn't already scale across windows and screen sizes, none of these surfaces will behave.
items.answer:
#### What survives
Your architecture already pays for itself here: repositories, use cases, ViewModels, and the Compose state model carry across all four surfaces unchanged. Nothing about these form factors changes your domain design. What changes is the presentation layer and the constraints each surface imposes.

#### Wear OS
Compose for Wear brings rotary input, Tiles, complications, and watch faces. You must handle the **ambient/always-on display** and treat battery and glanceability as first-class: the watch is for quick actions, and deep work stays in the phone companion app.

#### Android TV
Input is a D-pad, so **focus handling replaces touch**. Compose for TV provides focus-aware components, and the design is a content-centric 10-foot UI — rows of cards and previews, not dense lists. Voice search and the playback controls matter more than fine touch gestures.

#### Android Auto
The strictest case. While driving you get **template-based apps** through the car app library, and custom interactive UI is not allowed — media, messaging, and navigation are expressed through Google's templates. Distraction safety dictates every decision; there is no design freedom to trade.

#### Android XR
Your Compose UI is rendered into spatial panels in a 3D scene. Jetpack XR Compose handles windows, spatial layout, and gaze-and-hand input, and existing Compose content largely ports over — which is the payoff of the adaptive work.

#### The pattern
One codebase that scales across windows first, then thin per-surface UI layers. The phone app's layout quality is the prerequisite for all four.

code.caption: Shared state, then Wear vs TV presentation

followUps: Why is Android Auto's constraint set different from every other surface?
How does a 10-foot TV UI differ from touch-first design beyond input focus?
What role does adaptive design play before you ever target a new form factor?
traps: Answering as if each form factor is a new app — the architecture should already be form-factor agnostic.
Missing that Auto forbids custom UI entirely; it is template-only and distraction-safe by policy.

items.q: How do you implement Play Billing for a subscription? What are the moving parts? Where does server verification come in?
shortAnswer: The client uses the Play Billing library: `queryProductDetailsAsync`, then `launchBillingFlow` — and every purchase must be acknowledged within three days or it's refunded.
Subscriptions add base plans with layered offers, upgrades and downgrades with proration, and renewals on Google's infrastructure — your job is tracking the purchase-state transition.
The client is untrusted: your backend validates the purchase token against the Play Developer API and reacts to Real-Time Developer Notifications for renewals and cancellations.
items.answer:
#### The client flow
Everything starts from `ProductDetails`: query with `queryProductDetailsAsync(QueryProductDetailsParams)`, build `BillingFlowParams` with `setProductDetailsParamsList`, launch the flow from an activity, and handle the callback. Any purchase must be **acknowledged** (`acknowledgePurchase`) within three days of purchase or Google refunds it and revokes access. Acknowledge on the server once it has verified the token — that is the safe ordering.

#### Subscriptions are a state machine
A subscription is described by **base plans** (monthly, yearly) with **offers** layered on top. Purchases change over time: upgrades and downgrades use proration (`BillingFlowParams.ProrationMode`), and renewals happen on Google's infrastructure, not inside your app. Handle the `PENDING` purchase state — payment-method edge cases where the user has not finished paying — and decide what access they get in the meantime. Every new purchase carries a token that replaces the old one.

#### Server-side verification
The client is hostile territory. The app posts the `Purchase` token to your backend, which validates it against the **Google Play Developer API**. Better still, subscribe to **Real-Time Developer Notifications** (Cloud Pub/Sub) so your backend learns about renewals, cancellations, and refunds even when the app is closed. Your entitlements come from this server truth, never from a client-side boolean.

#### Policy and testing
Use license testing with your own test accounts, remember digital content must flow through Play billing (with real exceptions like physical goods), and keep the Data Safety form honest about what the purchase flow collects.

code.caption: Query a subscription and launch the billing flow

followUps: What does acknowledging a purchase actually protect against, and what happens if you do not?
How do you handle an upgrade with proration and a mid-cycle plan change?
Why is a PENDING purchase state important, and what access should the user get?
traps: Skipping acknowledgement — every subscription purchase must be acknowledged within three days or it is refunded.
Trusting client-side entitlement booleans; verification belongs on the server with the Play Developer API and RTDN.

items.q: How do you prompt users to update your app? How do you ask for a Play Store rating?
shortAnswer: In-app updates use `AppUpdateManager`: fetch update info, then `startUpdateFlowForResult` with `IMMEDIATE` or `FLEXIBLE` mode, routing the result through the activity-result callback.
`FLEXIBLE` lets the user keep using the app while the update downloads and installs on restart; `IMMEDIATE` blocks with a full-screen, non-dismissible flow.
In-app review is a separate `ReviewManager` flow that Google quota-limits: gate it on milestones, never every launch, and treat `ReviewErrorCode` as non-fatal.
items.answer:
#### In-app updates
`AppUpdateManager` is the entry point: `AppUpdateManagerFactory.create(context)` then `appUpdateInfo`. That tells you the `updateAvailability`, whether installation is allowed, and the **update priority** you set per rollout in the Play Console. When an update is available you call `startUpdateFlowForResult` with one of two strategies:
- **Immediate** — a full-screen, non-dismissible flow; use it when the update is critical (security fix, broken feature).
- **Flexible** — a non-blocking background download with a resume UI that installs on the next app restart; use it for routine releases.
Route the request code and `ActivityResult` through your activity-result handler: `RESULT_OK` means the user went along, `RESULT_CANCELED` means deferred — re-check state rather than caching it, and resurface flexibly later.

#### In-app review
A separate API. `ReviewManager.requestReviewFlow()` gives a `ReviewInfo`, then `launchReviewFlow(activity, reviewInfo)` shows Google's rating card. Quotas are enforced, so you can never force the dialog to appear — treat a `ReviewErrorCode` failure as non-fatal and re-attempt at a later milestone. Common practice: gate on meaningful achievements and throttle aggressively.

#### Design
Use the rollout priority flag for severity, respect the user's defer, and reserve immediate updates for cases where the cost of not updating is worse than the interruption.

code.caption: Update check plus a milestone-gated rating request

followUps: Immediate or flexible — how do you choose, and when is immediate actually justified?
What does the rollout priority flag control end to end?
Why can't you rely on the review dialog appearing, and how do you react to that?
traps: Requesting in-app review on every launch — quotas silently no-op it and it still annoys users.
Ignoring the activity result and assuming the update flow completed; the user can defer.

items.q: Why did Play move to App Bundles? How do Play Feature Delivery and Play Asset Delivery let you ship smaller?
shortAnswer: The App Bundle is what you upload; Play generates and signs the per-device APKs — base APK plus ABI, density, and language splits.
Play Feature Delivery splits code into dynamic features that install with the app, on demand, or conditionally, cutting the install-time download.
Play Asset Delivery serves large game-style assets as install-time, fast-follow, or on-demand packs, with texture-compression targeting so users only get the assets their GPU uses.
items.answer:
#### The App Bundle
You upload an `.aab`, not an APK. Play App Signing holds the app signing key, and Play generates a **base APK** plus configuration splits — one per ABI, density bucket, and language — so each install pulls only what its device needs. The bundle also solves a signing-rotation problem: the key stays with Google, so a leaked upload key no longer forces a whole migration.

#### Play Feature Delivery
Modules are declared with the `com.android.dynamic-feature` Gradle plugin. A feature can be **install-time** (part of the base experience), **on-demand** (downloaded when the user reaches it), or **conditional** (delivered by country, API level, or other criteria). On-demand features need `SplitCompat` so their code can be loaded after download, and state is tracked with `SplitInstallManager`. The payoff is a smaller initial download and an honest push toward modular architecture — features you cannot isolate are features you should not split.

#### Play Asset Delivery
Built for game-scale payloads: **install-time**, **fast-follow** (downloaded right after install, before first launch), or **on-demand** asset packs, each capped in size. You can target **texture-compression formats**, so a device only receives the ASTC/ETC2 assets its GPU supports — a real size saver for large games.

#### The trade-off
Smaller downloads and better ABI targeting cost complexity: more modules to build and test, and on-demand paths that must handle download failures, retries, and user cancellation.

code.caption: Installing an on-demand feature with SplitInstallManager

followUps: When would you choose on-demand over install-time delivery, and what breaks if you get it wrong?
How does the bundle approach change the way you test a release?
What does texture-compression targeting actually save, and for whom?
traps: Describing the bundle as a smaller APK — it is a delivery mechanism; Play still produces per-device APKs.
Forgetting SplitCompat for on-demand features, which crashes the app the moment code in a not-yet-installed module is touched.

items.q: Which Play policies gate a release for an Android engineer? How do you keep a release unblocked?
shortAnswer: The hard gates are mechanical and date-bound: `targetSdk 36` by 2026-08-31 (extension to 2026-11-01), and 16 KB page-size support for updates from 2027-02-01.
The second gate is behavioral: the Data Safety form, permissions policy, and content policies are enforced via review, and violations carry strikes.
Keep policy in the release loop — a policy checklist, staged rollouts, and Pre-launch reports — so problems surface before a full rollout.
items.answer:
#### What actually blocks you
The un-negotiable gates are checked at upload time. **Target API level**: apps below the requirement cannot be updated and new apps cannot be published — for the current train that means `targetSdk 36` required by **2026-08-31**, with an extension window to **2026-11-01**. **16 KB page sizes**: 16 KB-page devices are being enabled across the ecosystem, so apps and updates must support them from **2027-02-01** — practically, verify your native libraries and APK alignment, and test on 16 KB emulator images. Both are dates, not preferences.

#### Data safety and permissions
The Data Safety form and the permissions policy form the second gate: you declare what data you collect and how it is shared, and every requested permission must be necessary and demonstrably used. Enforcement here is retrospective — a form that is technically filed but inaccurate is a removal risk later. The Play Console also surfaces device-eligibility and policy findings to fix before rollout.

#### The reviewer gate
Content and behavior policies (prohibited content, ads, gambling, disclosures) are enforced by review and carry **strikes**. Strikes are account-level: an unresolved strike can pull an app, and repeated offenses can terminate the whole developer account.

#### Keeping releases unblocked
Treat policy as a CI gate. Keep a checklist — targetSdk, 16 KB readiness, data-safety declarations, permissions, compliance surface — run staged rollouts so you can pause, and let Pre-launch reports and coverage data catch issues before 100% of users get the build.

code.caption: The upload-time gates as build-time facts
Verify 16 KB page alignment on the built APK (policy from 2027-02-01)

followUps: What happens if you miss the targetSdk deadline, and is there any grace?
Why is the Data Safety form a release risk even when your code is compliant?
How do staged rollouts interact with policy enforcement and strikes?
traps: Treating policy as a legal-only concern; targetSdk and 16 KB alignment are hard, date-bound upload-time gates.
Not knowing strikes are account-level — a repeat offense can terminate the whole developer account, not just one app.

items.q: Where does Firebase fit in a modern Android stack? How do you make Crashlytics useful?
shortAnswer: Firebase is a managed backend: analytics, crash reporting, remote config, auth, Firestore, messaging, and functions — a strong default when speed beats infrastructure ownership.
The durable core is Analytics plus Crashlytics plus Remote Config; before adopting Firestore for core state, think hard about vendor lock-in, security rules, and cost.
Crashlytics is genuinely useful when every crash carries deobfuscated stacks, breadcrumbs, custom keys, and user context, and is correlated with releases and rollouts.
items.answer:
#### What the stack gives you
The durable core for a modern app is **Analytics + Crashlytics + Remote Config**: product signal, failure signal, and remote control without a release. Around that sit Auth, Firestore, Cloud Messaging, and Cloud Functions. The Firebase BoM keeps SDK versions aligned, and the integration seam is your `google-services.json` plus the build-time plugin wiring.

#### The architectural judgment
The right answer is *partial* adoption. Analytics, crash reporting, and configuration are commodity capabilities with no upside to self-host — use Firebase there without guilt. For core business state, you are coupling your schema, security rules, and pricing to Google's platform. Decide deliberately where the data layer lives, and structure code so the storage choice is replaceable.

#### Making Crashlytics useful
- **Deobfuscation**: upload R8/ProGuard mappings so stack traces are readable — symbol-less traces turn triage into guessing.
- **Context**: `crashlytics.log()` breadcrumbs, `setCustomKey()` for state, `setUserId()` for repro, and `recordException()` for non-fatal errors you actually want to track.
- **Actionability**: tie crashes to releases and rollouts, set up issue alerts, and remember that 'no crash' is not the same as 'no problem' — some of your worst bugs are silent.
- **Privacy**: wire `setDataCollectionEnabled(false)` to your consent flow rather than sending everything by default.

code.caption: Attaching context to a crash and honoring consent

followUps: When would you move beyond Firebase and build your own backend?
What does a fatal vs non-fatal distinction change about your alerting?
How does deobfuscation interact with the app bundle, and why do symbol-less stacks break triage?
traps: Treating Crashlytics as just a crash reporter — without mappings, breadcrumbs, and release correlation it produces noise, not signal.
Adopting Firestore for core state without discussing vendor lock-in, security rules, and cost.

items.q: What is the Privacy Sandbox on Android? What changed about the advertising ID that a mobile engineer must know?
shortAnswer: The Privacy Sandbox replaces cross-app tracking with privacy-preserving APIs — Topics, Protected Audience, Attribution Reporting — plus an SDK Runtime isolating ad-tech code.
The advertising ID is no longer a stable key: it needs `ACCESS_ADSERVICES_AD_ID`, resets on opt-out, and ships disabled on Android 16+.
That means anything keyed on the ad ID gets replaced by first-party identity, server-side aggregation, and measurement fallbacks — design for the all-zeros case.
items.answer:
#### The advertising ID problem
`AdvertisingIdClient` let any app with the `AD_ID` permission read a stable, reset-able identifier and combine it across apps into profiles — exactly the cross-app tracking the Privacy Sandbox exists to end. On Android 13+ reading it already requires `ACCESS_ADSERVICES_AD_ID`; after user opt-out or reset the API returns zeros. On **Android 16+, new devices ship with the ad ID disabled by default**, with users able to opt back in via Google's ads settings — so treating it as a stable identity key breaks by design.

#### The Privacy Sandbox APIs
- **Topics** — coarse, on-device interest signals per app, with no cross-app linking by the platform.
- **Protected Audience** — on-device ad selection and remarketing without shipping user lists to ad tech at runtime.
- **Attribution Reporting** — aggregate, differentially-private conversion measurement.
- **SDK Runtime** — ad SDKs run through isolated APIs so an embedded SDK cannot scrape your whole app context.
These land in waves across API levels, availability is platform- and consent-gated, and the app does not get to decide when they are enabled.

#### What you must change
Anything keying measurement or identity off the ad ID is now a liability. Rework attribution around first-party IDs and server-side aggregation, adopt `AdvertisingServices`-aware SDKs, and make consent flows honest about data sharing. Validate every pipeline against the all-zeros case — that is the default state on the newest devices, not an edge case.

code.caption: Reading the ad ID today — permission-gated and opt-out aware

followUps: How do Topics differ from an interest profile built from a tracking ID?
What breaks first when you remove the ad ID from your analytics pipeline?
How does the SDK Runtime change what an embedded ad SDK can observe?
traps: Treating the ad ID as a stable identity key — on Android 16+ it is disabled by default and reads zeros.
Confusing the Privacy Sandbox with an API you opt into; availability is platform- and consent-gated and the rollout is phased.

items.q: Your app runs on phones only. What does it take to meet the large-screen and foldable quality guidelines?
shortAnswer: The bar is adaptive layout, not separate builds: UI responds to `WindowSizeClass` (Compact, Medium, Expanded) and reflows across a foldable's postures.
Use Compose's adaptive Material3 scaffolds — `ListDetailPaneScaffold` and `SupportingPaneScaffold` with pane expansion — rather than hardcoded phone breakpoints.
The guidelines grade actual behavior: no letterboxing, no orientation lock on foldables, proper resizability, and full keyboard, mouse, and stylus input support.
items.answer:
#### The baseline: resizable windows
Quality starts with **window size classes** — `WindowSizeClass` (Compact, Medium, Expanded) from the adaptive library — because a foldable changes the window metrics mid-session. Layouts branch on the class, and the classes drive Material3 adaptive scaffolds: `ListDetailPaneScaffold`, `SupportingPaneScaffold`, and the adaptive `NavigationSuite`. That is the difference between 'it scales' (a phone layout stretched) and 'it uses the space' (a real second pane appears).

#### Foldables specifically
Unfolding produces a **resize/config change, not an activity recreation** — your ViewModel and saved state must survive it. Handle the hinge through the WindowManager library's `WindowInfoTracker`/`FoldingFeature` (state: flat, half-open, full-open, plus occlusion and hinge bounds), keep critical UI clear of the hinge and safe areas, and do not lock orientation on foldables.

#### What the guidelines actually test
Play evaluates real behavior against the quality criteria: no letterboxing, correct resizability across the supported size range, and the full input ecosystem — keyboard navigation, focus order, mouse, and stylus. Testing is the other half: emulator size presets, the foldable emulator's posture states, and running every screen at all three size classes.

#### The architecture takeaway
Hoist pane-level state so list and detail are independently saveable, let the adaptive scaffold own the two-pane switch, and the domain layer never learns that a size class exists.

code.caption: Window size class branching, and hinge posture from WindowInfo

followUps: Why is WindowSizeClass better than hardcoded breakpoints?
What breaks if you lock orientation on a foldable?
How is a size-class change different from an activity recreation, and what survives it?
traps: Claiming 'it scales' while the app just stretches a phone layout — the guideline bar is using the extra space with real panes.
Forgetting that unfolding is a config/resize event your ViewModel and saved state must survive without a restart.

items.q: Why is accessibility a shipping requirement? What is the minimum bar for an Android engineer?
shortAnswer: Accessibility is a legal and product requirement — WCAG-style compliance and Play's quality expectations — and it's good engineering that benefits every user.
The minimum bar: every image has a `contentDescription` or is decorative, elements have names and roles, touch targets are at least 48dp, contrast sufficient.
Compose derives semantics from components for free; extend them with `semantics {}`, roles, and `clearAndSetSemantics {}`, then verify with TalkBack and the Accessibility Scanner.
items.answer:
#### Why it is a requirement
Accessibility is a shipping condition, not a feature. Software accessibility has regulatory teeth (WCAG and its equivalents), Play's quality expectations call it out, and enterprises will not approve a product that fails it. The engineering case is the durable one: better semantics, targets, and contrast improve usability for everyone — the elderly user, the user in bright glare, the one-thumb user.

#### The minimum bar — a practical checklist
- Every meaningful `Image`/`Icon` has a `contentDescription`; decorative ones are explicitly null.
- Every interactive element exposes a name and role. Compose does this by default for `Button`, `Checkbox`, and friends; custom clickables need `semantics { role = Role.Button }`.
- Touch targets are at least 48dp — Material does this, a raw `Modifier.clickable` may not.
- Text contrast is at least 4.5:1 for body copy, and no information is conveyed by color alone.
- Focus order is meaningful, and custom views implement `onInitializeAccessibilityEvent`.

#### How you verify
Do not assume — run TalkBack over the real user flows, including dialogs and error states; run the Accessibility Scanner; and inspect Compose's semantics tree with the testing APIs. Build it into the definition of done. Retrofitting accessibility after launch is the expensive way to do it, and it is where the risk actually lives.

code.caption: Accessible images and custom clickables

followUps: What does Compose give you from the semantics tree, and what still needs manual work?
How would you test accessibility in CI?
When is a contentDescription wrong, and what should it actually say?
traps: Treating accessibility as a post-launch hardening task; both the cost and the risk are lower when it is in the definition of done.
Thinking 'I used Material components so it is accessible' — custom clickables, images, and merged/traversed semantics are where it actually breaks.
